name: ResourceQuota: compute & objects
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration and Security. Drill EVERY corner of namespace resource governance harder than the exam: compute ResourceQuota, object-count quota, scoped quota (BestEffort), LimitRange defaults, LimitRange min/max bounds, ratio limits, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix of a pod rejected by a quota. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: ResourceQuota — cap total compute
questions.teach:
A **ResourceQuota** caps a namespace's totals. A *compute* quota tracks `requests.cpu`, `requests.memory`, `limits.cpu`, `limits.memory`. Create it with `kubectl create quota <name> --hard=... -n <ns>`.

**Gotcha:** the four keys use dots (`requests.cpu`) — in jsonpath you must escape them (`spec.hard.requests\.cpu`).
questions.prompt:
In namespace `ckad-quotas`, create a ResourceQuota named `compute-quota` with hard limits: `requests.cpu=1`, `requests.memory=1Gi`, `limits.cpu=2`, `limits.memory=2Gi`.

Target: `compute-quota` shows exactly those four hard values.

verification.description: compute-quota has the four compute hard limits (1/1Gi/2/2Gi)

questions.eli5:
Think of a namespace as a shared apartment, and the whole cluster as the building with a fixed power supply. A **ResourceQuota** is the breaker box for your apartment: it sets a hard ceiling on how much electricity (CPU and memory) everyone in that apartment is allowed to draw in total.

A *compute* quota watches four meters at once:

- **requests.cpu / requests.memory** — the power you *reserve* up front (your guaranteed slice).
- **limits.cpu / limits.memory** — the most power you're *allowed to spike to*.

`kubectl create quota compute-quota --hard=requests.cpu=1,requests.memory=1Gi,limits.cpu=2,limits.memory=2Gi -n ckad-quotas` installs that breaker box. From then on, Kubernetes adds up every pod's requests and limits in the namespace and refuses anything that would trip a breaker.

**Watch out for:**

- The four keys use **dots**: `requests.cpu`, `limits.memory`. In jsonpath those dots are part of the name, so you must escape them: `{.spec.hard.requests\.cpu}` — otherwise jsonpath thinks `requests` and `cpu` are two separate steps and finds nothing.
- Memory values are case- and unit-sensitive: `1Gi` (binary, 1024-based) is **not** `1G` (decimal, 1000-based). Match the unit the task asks for.
- A quota only governs the **one namespace** it lives in. It does nothing to pods in other namespaces.
- Creating the quota doesn't move existing pods; it only gates **new** admissions and current totals.
questions.deepDive:
## ResourceQuota (compute) — full rundown

### Mental model
A **ResourceQuota** is a namespace-scoped admission gate plus a running tally. It (1) tracks the *sum* of a resource across all objects in one namespace and (2) **rejects** any create/update that would push a total past its `hard` cap. Compute quotas govern CPU and memory **requests** and **limits**.

### Create it
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas create quota compute-quota \
  --hard=requests.cpu=1,requests.memory=1Gi,limits.cpu=2,limits.memory=2Gi
```
Equivalent YAML:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
```

### The four compute keys
| Key | Caps the sum of… | Aliases |
|---|---|---|
| `requests.cpu` | every container's `resources.requests.cpu` | `cpu` (bare = requests.cpu) |
| `requests.memory` | every container's `resources.requests.memory` | `memory` |
| `limits.cpu` | every container's `resources.limits.cpu` | — |
| `limits.memory` | every container's `resources.limits.memory` | — |

> Bare `cpu`/`memory` in a quota are **synonyms for the requests** form. Prefer the explicit `requests.*` names on the exam.

### Inspecting usage
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get resourcequota
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota compute-quota   # shows Used vs Hard per key
# jsonpath — note the ESCAPED dots:
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get quota compute-quota \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.hard.requests\.cpu}{"\n"}'
```
`describe` output:
```
Name:            compute-quota
Resource         Used   Hard
--------         ----   ----
limits.cpu       0      2
limits.memory    0      2Gi
requests.cpu     0      1
requests.memory  0      1Gi
```

### Units refresher
| Written | Means |
|---|---|
| `1` / `1000m` (cpu) | 1 core (`m` = millicores) |
| `500m` (cpu) | half a core |
| `1Gi` | 1024³ bytes (binary) |
| `1G` | 1000³ bytes (decimal) |
| `256Mi` | 256 × 1024² bytes |

### The enforcement rule (critical)
Once a compute quota tracks a resource, **every new pod MUST declare both a request AND a limit for that resource**, or admission rejects it (`must specify requests.cpu`, etc.). A LimitRange with defaults can satisfy this automatically — covered in the LimitRange lab.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Escape the dots in jsonpath**: `requests\.cpu` is one key, not a path. `{.spec.hard.requests.cpu}` returns nothing.
- `1Gi` ≠ `1G`. Unit mismatches silently fail an exact-value check.
- Quota is **per-namespace**; it never crosses namespaces.
- Quota gates admission going forward — it does not evict pods already running when it was created, but existing usage *does* count toward the totals.
- Multiple ResourceQuotas can coexist in one namespace; a pod must satisfy **all** of them.
- Editing a running pod's resources is mostly immutable — recreate rather than patch.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas create quota compute-quota \
  --hard=requests.cpu=1,requests.memory=1Gi,limits.cpu=2,limits.memory=2Gi
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota compute-quota
```

questions.title: A pod that fits under the compute quota
questions.teach:
Once a compute quota tracks a resource, **every new pod must declare both requests AND limits** for that resource or admission rejects it. Give the container a `resources:` block with values that fit under the quota.

**Gotcha:** omit even one dimension (e.g. `limits.memory`) and the pod is rejected with `must specify limits.memory`.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-quotas`, create pod `fits` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container name `app`) with `requests` cpu `200m` / memory `256Mi` and `limits` cpu `500m` / memory `512Mi`. It must be admitted and reach Running.

Target: pod `fits` is Running and declares exactly those requests and limits.
questions.hint: Write YAML with a full `resources` block (both requests and limits, all four values) and apply it.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: fits, namespace: ckad-quotas }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
YAML

verification.description: pod 'fits' is Running with exact requests 200m/256Mi + limits 500m/512Mi

questions.eli5:
Now that the apartment has a breaker box (the compute quota), there's a new house rule for anyone moving a new appliance (pod) in: you must **declare how much power it reserves and the most it could ever spike to** — for *both* electricity (CPU) and memory. No declaration, no entry.

This pod plays by the rules. Its one container (`app`) says:

- **requests**: cpu `200m` (reserve a fifth of a core), memory `256Mi`.
- **limits**: cpu `500m` (never spike past half a core), memory `512Mi`.

Add those up against the quota's ceilings (requests 1 cpu / 1Gi, limits 2 cpu / 2Gi) and everything fits comfortably, so the doorman (admission controller) lets it in and the pod reaches `Running`.

**Watch out for:**

- **All four values are mandatory** once a compute quota exists. Leave out even one — say `limits.memory` — and the pod is bounced with `must specify limits.memory`. You get requests *and* limits, cpu *and* memory, or nothing.
- The pod must actually **fit**: your requests/limits added to what's already used can't exceed the ceilings, or it's rejected for exceeding quota.
- Requests ≤ limits, always. A request bigger than its limit is invalid.
- A rejected pod from a bare `kubectl run` just fails with an error; a rejected pod inside a Deployment leaves the Deployment stuck at `0/1` (you have to dig into the ReplicaSet to see why).
- Match the exact numbers and units the task names — `256Mi` is not `256M`.
questions.deepDive:
## Admitting a pod under a compute quota — full rundown

### Mental model
A compute ResourceQuota flips on a **mandatory-declaration rule**: for every resource the quota tracks, each container in a new pod must set *both* `requests` and `limits`. The quota then checks the pod's totals against remaining headroom. Two independent gates: **completeness** (did you declare everything?) and **capacity** (does it fit?).

### The pod
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: fits
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
```
```bash
kubectl apply -f fits.yaml
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get pod fits -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota compute-quota   # Used now reflects this pod
```

### Does it fit? (against hard = requests 1 cpu/1Gi, limits 2 cpu/2Gi)
| Dimension | This pod | Quota hard | Headroom |
|---|---|---|---|
| requests.cpu | 200m | 1 (1000m) | ✅ 800m left |
| requests.memory | 256Mi | 1Gi (1024Mi) | ✅ 768Mi left |
| limits.cpu | 500m | 2 (2000m) | ✅ 1500m left |
| limits.memory | 512Mi | 2Gi | ✅ 1536Mi left |

### requests vs limits
- **requests** = guaranteed reservation; the scheduler uses it to place the pod and it's what `requests.*` quota keys sum.
- **limits** = hard ceiling; CPU is throttled at the limit, memory over the limit → **OOMKilled**.
- Invariant: `request ≤ limit` per resource, or the pod spec is invalid.

### Rejection messages you must recognise
| Cause | Error |
|---|---|
| Missing a dimension | `pods "x" is forbidden: failed quota: compute-quota: must specify limits.memory,requests.cpu` |
| Exceeds capacity | `exceeded quota: compute-quota, requested: requests.cpu=…, used: …, limited: …` |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Partial resources are rejected**, not auto-filled (unless a LimitRange supplies defaults). All tracked dimensions are required.
- A bare `kubectl run` won't let you set both requests and limits easily — write YAML, or use `--requests`/`--limits` flags (deprecated in newer kubectl). YAML is safest on the exam.
- `256Mi` ≠ `256M`; `512Mi` ≠ `0.5Gi` for an exact-string grader even though the bytes differ.
- When the rejected pod is owned by a Deployment/ReplicaSet, the pod never appears — diagnose via `kubectl describe rs` or `kubectl get events`.
- Admission re-checks on every create; a pod that fit yesterday may be rejected today if other pods consumed the headroom.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl apply -f fits.yaml     # resources block with BOTH requests & limits
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get pod fits -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota compute-quota
```

questions.title: ResourceQuota — cap object counts
questions.teach:
A ResourceQuota can also cap the **number of objects**. Built-in count names include `pods`, `services`, `secrets`, `configmaps`; a generic form is `count/<resource>.<group>` (e.g. `count/deployments.apps`). `--hard=configmaps=3` allows at most three.

**Gotcha:** counts are **current live objects**, not cumulative — delete an object and the slot frees up.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-quotas`, create a ResourceQuota named `object-quota` with hard counts: `configmaps=3` and `count/deployments.apps=2`.

Target: `object-quota` has hard `configmaps: 3` and `count/deployments.apps: 2`.
questions.eli5:
A quota doesn't only watch *power* — it can also limit *how many of a thing* you're allowed to have at once, like a rule that says "this apartment may keep at most 3 houseplants and at most 2 bicycles." That's an **object-count quota**: it counts live Kubernetes objects instead of CPU or memory.

Here you set two caps in one quota:

- `configmaps=3` — at most three ConfigMaps in the namespace.
- `count/deployments.apps=2` — at most two Deployments (from the `apps` API group).

`kubectl create quota object-quota --hard=configmaps=3,count/deployments.apps=2 -n ckad-quotas` installs it.

Some common objects have **short built-in names** (`pods`, `services`, `secrets`, `configmaps`). For anything else you use the generic form **`count/<resource>.<group>`** — that's why Deployments are written `count/deployments.apps` (they live in the `apps` group).

**Watch out for:**

- Counts are of **currently existing** objects, not a running total. Delete a ConfigMap and that slot frees up again — it's "how many right now," not "how many ever."
- The `count/<resource>.<group>` spelling is exact: plural resource, a dot, then the API group (`deployments.apps`, `cronjobs.batch`). A core-group object uses `count/<resource>` with no group (e.g. `count/pods`), though short names like `pods` also work.
- The cap is **inclusive**: `configmaps=3` means three is fine, the fourth is refused.
- This still only applies inside its own namespace.
questions.deepDive:
## Object-count ResourceQuota — full rundown

### Mental model
Besides compute, a ResourceQuota can cap the **number of live objects** of a kind in a namespace. Two spellings exist: a handful of **built-in short names**, and the generic **`count/<resource>.<group>`** form that works for (almost) any resource type.

### Create it
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas create quota object-quota \
  --hard=configmaps=3,count/deployments.apps=2
```
YAML:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: object-quota
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  hard:
    configmaps: "3"
    count/deployments.apps: "2"
```

### Built-in short count names (core group)
| Short name | Counts |
|---|---|
| `pods` | pods (non-terminal) |
| `services` | Services |
| `services.loadbalancers` | LoadBalancer-type Services |
| `services.nodeports` | NodePort-type Services |
| `secrets` | Secrets |
| `configmaps` | ConfigMaps |
| `persistentvolumeclaims` | PVCs |
| `replicationcontrollers` | RCs |
| `resourcequotas` | ResourceQuotas |

### Generic form: `count/<resource>.<group>`
For anything without a short name, use the plural resource name + API group:
| Object | Count key |
|---|---|
| Deployment | `count/deployments.apps` |
| ReplicaSet | `count/replicasets.apps` |
| StatefulSet | `count/statefulsets.apps` |
| Job | `count/jobs.batch` |
| CronJob | `count/cronjobs.batch` |
| Pod (core group) | `count/pods` (no group) |
| Ingress | `count/ingresses.networking.k8s.io` |

> Core-group resources drop the group: `count/pods`, `count/services`. For non-core, the group is mandatory: `count/deployments.apps`.

### Inspect
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota object-quota
# Resource                 Used   Hard
# configmaps               1      3       (the default 'kube-root-ca.crt' counts!)
# count/deployments.apps   0      2
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get quota object-quota \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.hard.count/deployments\.apps}{"\n"}'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Counts are live, not cumulative.** Deleting an object frees its slot immediately; the quota tracks current state.
- The default **`kube-root-ca.crt` ConfigMap** exists in every namespace and already consumes one `configmaps` slot — budget for it.
- Group spelling is exact: `.apps`, `.batch`, `.networking.k8s.io`. Wrong or missing group → the key tracks nothing (always shows `Used 0`).
- Cap is **inclusive of the limit**: `configmaps=3` admits the 3rd, rejects the 4th.
- jsonpath: escape every dot — `count/deployments\.apps`.
- The whole `count/*` key itself contains a `/` and `.`; quote it in YAML as a string key.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas create quota object-quota \
  --hard=configmaps=3,count/deployments.apps=2
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota object-quota
```

questions.title: Scoped ResourceQuota (BestEffort)
questions.teach:
A quota can apply **only to a subset of pods** via `scopes`. `BestEffort` matches pods with NO resource requests/limits; `NotBestEffort`, `Terminating`, `NotTerminating` are the others. `kubectl create quota ... --scopes=BestEffort`.

**Gotcha:** a `BestEffort` quota may only set `pods` (count) — it can't cap cpu/memory, since BestEffort pods have none.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-quotas`, create a ResourceQuota named `be-quota` scoped to `BestEffort`, with hard `pods=1`.

Target: `be-quota` has hard `pods: 1` and `spec.scopes` contains `BestEffort`.

verification.description: be-quota: hard pods=1 scoped to BestEffort

questions.eli5:
Sometimes you don't want a quota to apply to *everyone* in the apartment — only to a certain **kind** of tenant. A **scoped quota** is a rule with a bouncer that checks each pod against a guest list and only counts the ones that match.

The scope here is **BestEffort**. A "BestEffort" pod is one that declares **no** CPU or memory requests or limits at all — the freeloader that grabs whatever's spare. This quota says: *"Of those no-reservation pods, allow at most 1."* Pods that *do* declare resources are simply ignored by this quota.

`kubectl create quota be-quota --hard=pods=1 --scopes=BestEffort -n ckad-quotas` sets it up.

The four scopes you can pick from:

- **BestEffort** — pods with no requests/limits.
- **NotBestEffort** — pods that *do* set requests/limits.
- **Terminating** — pods with an `activeDeadlineSeconds`.
- **NotTerminating** — pods without one.

**Watch out for:**

- A **BestEffort** quota can only cap **`pods`** (a count). It cannot set cpu/memory ceilings — BestEffort pods have no resource numbers to measure, so those keys are meaningless and rejected.
- The scope decides *which pods are counted*, not whether they're allowed in general. A non-matching pod isn't blocked by this quota at all.
- Scope names are case-sensitive and exact: `BestEffort`, not `besteffort`.
- `BestEffort` and `NotBestEffort` are opposites — a pod is always exactly one of them.
questions.deepDive:
## Scoped ResourceQuota — full rundown

### Mental model
`scopes` narrow a quota so it only **counts pods that match a filter**. A scoped quota is invisible to non-matching pods. `BestEffort` matches pods that declare *zero* CPU/memory requests and limits.

### Create it
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas create quota be-quota --hard=pods=1 --scopes=BestEffort
```
YAML:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: be-quota
  namespace: ckad-quotas
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "1"
  scopes:
  - BestEffort
```

### The four classic scopes
| Scope | Matches pods that… | Compatible hard keys |
|---|---|---|
| `BestEffort` | set **no** requests/limits at all | **only `pods`** |
| `NotBestEffort` | set *some* request/limit (Burstable or Guaranteed) | compute + `pods` |
| `Terminating` | have `spec.activeDeadlineSeconds >= 0` | compute + `pods` |
| `NotTerminating` | have no `activeDeadlineSeconds` | compute + `pods` |

> `BestEffort`/`NotBestEffort` are a partition, as are `Terminating`/`NotTerminating`.

### QoS classes (what "BestEffort" means)
| QoS class | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Guaranteed** | every container sets requests == limits for cpu AND memory |
| **Burstable** | at least one request/limit set, but not Guaranteed |
| **BestEffort** | **no** requests or limits anywhere in the pod |

`BestEffort` scope == pods in the BestEffort QoS class.

### Why BestEffort can only cap `pods`
BestEffort pods have no cpu/memory numbers. Putting `requests.cpu` in a `BestEffort`-scoped quota is rejected:
```
unsupported scope "BestEffort" for resource "requests.cpu"
```
So a BestEffort quota's only meaningful lever is the pod **count**.

### scopeSelector (the richer, operator-based form)
Beyond the four named scopes, `scopeSelector` supports `PriorityClass` matching:
```yaml
spec:
  hard: { pods: "10" }
  scopeSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - scopeName: PriorityClass
      operator: In          # In | NotIn | Exists | DoesNotExist
      values: ["high"]
```

### Inspect
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get quota be-quota -o jsonpath='{.spec.scopes}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n ckad-quotas describe quota be-quota
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- A **BestEffort** quota that sets anything other than `pods` is rejected — don't add cpu/memory.
- Scope names are **case-sensitive**: `BestEffort`, `NotTerminating`.
- Scopes filter *which* pods count; they don't block non-matching pods — those are governed by other (unscoped) quotas.
- A pod with even a single request (e.g. only `requests.cpu`) is **Burstable**, not BestEffort, so a BestEffort quota ignores it.
- Multiple quotas apply simultaneously; a pod must satisfy every quota whose scope it matches.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ckad-quotas create quota be-quota --hard=pods=1 --scopes=BestEffort
kubectl -n ckad-quotas get quota be-quota -o jsonpath='{.spec.scopes}'
```
